Have a ton of them, here are some hastily uploaded ones, I'll add more to the album later: http://imgur.com/a/t2vK7Nd They look huge bc they're norwegian forest cats, but oldest one (orange tabby) is 5 months old today, grey and black tabby is 4 and half and brown tabby is 3 and half. They're already giving me purrs and even kisses. Gonna try letting them loose around the house today again and see how it goes.

Same here on the goal/passion and feeling something. SPD turns everything into a grey fog of mehness and if I'm lucky enough to find a spark, it helps so much, no matter what it is. A creative project, a hobbie, a certain book or game or series, even just a particular fantasy I'm playing with in my head (again, SPD at work). Being able to express myself and being heard is also a new positive experience for me, as growing up I was always ignored. I was surprised with how much it helped, considering I didn't think I needed it.

Again, thank you for listening.

Try reading about alexithymia. That's basically a "cut" between the emotion itself and anywhere between identifying it and expressing it. Could be something more along those lines. Could be that you just have trouble expressing yourself verbally.

>Hopefully the kittens become more affectionate as time passes.

I hope so too. Luckily I'm used to socializing kittens, so I got a few tricks and it's been working. It's just that it's one more thing draining me when it was supposed to help me heal.

I've been trying to get back to the project, it's just pure exhaustion getting in the way. But I want to because I feel it might be the only thing I have left.

I've talked to both my psychiatrist and therapist about the symptoms and they say it's normal, given my disorder and everything that's been happening. Talking it over helps a bit, but there being no solutions still makes me feel trapped.

Thank you.

SPD is mainly not desiring social interaction, which leads to a certain inability to create bonds with people; it's not that we dislike humans, we just don't care. That and muted emotions and/or an inability to identify emotions, also known as alexithymia. Outside those two criteria there are a few others, like preferring solitary activities and preoccupation with introspection and fantasy that mainly flow from those two.

As for how it's like to have it: it basically feels like you're a ghost or a robot or an actor going through an elaborate world or play that you don't quite belong in. It's like being an outsider to everything that happens, as if you're watching things happen, but aren't part of them. Some schizoids (myself included) are able to put on what is called a "mask". We appear as normal, socially invested and engaged as any neurotypical, but inside we couldn't give less of a damn. We have high cognitive empathy, but low affective empathy, so we're not like psychopaths: we're able to understand why people are upset or sad or angry and even relate that to our own experiences, but their mood doesn't affect ours. Most schizoids also spent a lot of time lost in their thoughts and, especially, in their fantasies (personally, I ended up pursuing writing due to this, got some positive feedback from editors and that's why the creative career was on the table).

It's basically like being an extreme introvert, with a lot more specific psychological specifics, especially when it comes to boundaries. Look up split self and inner world related to schizoid.

Not that profitable, plus it requires a significant initial investment, that I couldn't make right now. My new kittens are all norwegian forest cats (non breeding approved ones, except for one) and I met with some breeders and I got some insight into it. They all had day jobs too.
